subtitle: Leaders can address microaggressions in everyday interactions with clarity, care and appropriate follow-through. The approach avoids guessing at motives or placing the burden on the person affected.
scope: For DHS leaders and supervisors. Learning activities use practice interactions and do not determine whether a real incident meets a legal or policy standard. Follow current agency procedures, applicable workplace policies and responsible HR guidance for actual concerns. Do not put real personnel details or inferred cultural orientations in course responses.
introTranscript: A comment can sound ordinary to one person and communicate exclusion to another. Leaders need a way to notice the interaction, respond proportionately, hear the relevant experience and follow through through the right process. The term microaggression does not make the effect trivial, and it does not remove the need for evidence or a fair response. This course practices specific language and work decisions without diagnosing motives from identity. You will distinguish immediate action from formal handling, avoid making a colleague educate the team, and review whether workplace arrangements improve. The consultant offers guidance and feedback; leaders retain the responsibilities of their roles.

lessons.title: Notice the interaction before naming the motive
lessons.summary: Separate the words or action, the reported effect and an explanation that still needs evidence.
lessons.objective: Describe a practice interaction using observable words or actions.
objectives: Describe a practice interaction using observable words or actions.
Distinguish reported effect from an unsupported claim about motive.
Identify when current policy scope and responsible guidance are needed.
takeaways: Intent and effect are different questions.
A course does not adjudicate an incident.
lessons.statement: You can take an effect seriously without claiming to know everything about the speaker’s intent.

image.caption: A specific account makes the interaction easier to examine and address.

intro.heading: Begin with what happened
intro.body:
A leader hears an unfamiliar-name joke and notices that a colleague stops contributing. One person says it was harmless; another says it shows deliberate hostility. Both explanations may arrive before anyone has described the actual words and context. A responsible response begins with the observable interaction and what is reported about its effect. It does not require the leader to infer motive from a person’s identity or dismiss the concern because the speaker intended humor.

Microaggressions can involve comments, behaviors or interactions that communicate bias or exclusion. The State of Minnesota Respectful Workplace policy includes the term, while also distinguishing its own scope from policies addressing protected-class and sexual-harassment matters. Use current agency guidance to identify the responsible process for an actual concern. The learning label does not decide which policy applies or establish a legal outcome.

Describe the action carefully. What was said or done? Where and in what work context? What did you observe, and what did the affected person choose to report? Separate these from guesses such as “they are too sensitive” or “the speaker must be malicious.” A fair description can support an appropriate response without minimizing the experience or making a premature finding.

Consider relevant context without using it as an automatic excuse. A misunderstanding may need clarification; a repeated pattern may raise a different question; a serious incident may require prompt designated handling. Do not create a rule that a person must experience several incidents before receiving support. Ask responsible offices about actual duties and routes rather than inventing thresholds in the course.

Keep real records and personal information in approved channels. These exercises use invented examples so you can practice a clear account and next step. The aim is to improve leadership judgment: notice, describe, respond and obtain the appropriate guidance, while preserving dignity and responsibility for everyone involved.

lessons.keyStatement: A specific account is more useful than a confident label about either person.

flashcards.back: A comment, behavior or interaction that may communicate bias or exclusion; actual concerns require the applicable evidence and responsible process.
A supported description of what was said or done, distinct from an explanation of motive.
The consequence or experience reported or observed in the situation.
What a person meant to do; it should not be assumed from identity or used to erase an effect.
The current agency process or office appropriate for an actual workplace concern.

items.title: “It was just a joke”
items.body: A stated intention is relevant, but it does not establish that the interaction had no effect. Ask what was said and why the concern matters to the work. Avoid turning the conversation into a demand that the affected person prove harm publicly before the leader responds appropriately.

items.title: “They are too sensitive”
items.body: This labels the person rather than examining the interaction. Describe the words and reported effect, and seek the appropriate guidance. People can have different experiences without one account being automatically invalid. A fair process does not begin by dismissing the person who raised the concern.

items.title: “I know the motive”
items.body: You may have a concern about the behavior without knowing its motive. Keep the distinction clear and use the responsible process for actual findings. Identity, familiarity or one impression should not replace evidence. An immediate practical response can occur while formal questions are routed appropriately.

tabs.label: Words or action
tabs.body: Words or action describe the interaction in a form that can be examined. A name-related remark and a character diagnosis are different kinds of statements. Use accurate context in actual approved records and invented detail here. This helps the leader address behavior without pretending to know motivation or every relevant fact from a single exchange.

tabs.label: Effect
tabs.body: Effect identifies the observed or reported consequence and the scope of the account. A colleague may report being singled out, while the meeting record shows their contribution was interrupted. Take each seriously without claiming all community members share the experience. The work effect can guide an appropriate response even while other facts remain uncertain.

tabs.label: Next question
tabs.body: A next question identifies the practical response and responsible process needed. A course label does not establish a policy violation or legal outcome. Ask what expectation can be addressed now and what must be reported or handled elsewhere. This allows action without dismissing the concern because a complete formal finding is not yet available.

check.question: A leader hears a comment and an employee reports feeling singled out. What can the leader do without assuming motive?
check.correct: Describe the interaction, take the reported effect seriously and use responsible guidance to decide the appropriate response and process.
wrong: Dismiss the report because the speaker called it a joke.
Diagnose the speaker’s cultural orientation from the comment.
Declare a legal outcome without examining the facts or applicable process.
check.feedbackCorrect: This keeps observation, experience and formal determination distinct while allowing appropriate action.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Calling the interaction a joke does not erase the reported effect. A remark cannot establish the speaker’s assessed intercultural orientation. Declaring a legal outcome skips the applicable facts and process. Describe the interaction, take the account seriously and use responsible guidance to connect an appropriate response with actual duties.

items.text: The colleague’s name was shortened after they asked for the full name to be used.
The colleague says the repeated exchange made contribution difficult.
The colleague is too sensitive to work with the team.
The leader heard the words during the review meeting.
The participant says they felt singled out by the introduction.
The speaker’s identity proves deliberate hostility.

lessons.next: Next, practice a proportionate response in the moment.

scenario.context: DSD practice case: During a review, Bruno jokes about shortening Zainab’s name after she has asked colleagues to use it correctly. Supervisor Imani hears the words. Bruno says he intended friendliness; Zainab says the exchange makes it harder to participate.
options: Tell Zainab she should appreciate the friendly intent.
Describe and address the interaction appropriately, take the effect seriously and follow the current responsible process for any formal concern.
Assign Bruno an IDI orientation from the exchange.
responses: Intent does not erase the stated participation concern.
This makes the interaction and next responsibility clear without claiming a complete motive or legal finding.
An interaction is not a licensed assessment or a basis for a personal cultural label.

lessons.transfer: Describe an invented interaction with observed words, reported effect, what remains unknown and an appropriate process question.

move.control: You can notice and describe the interaction accurately without diagnosing either person.
move.failure: A leader chooses a personal label instead of examining what happened and what response is needed.
move.next: In the next relevant situation, separate the observation from the first explanation before responding.

lessons.title: Respond in the moment without creating a spectacle
lessons.summary: Use a brief, clear intervention suited to the situation while preserving safety and formal responsibilities.
lessons.objective: Write a brief response that addresses a specific interaction and returns to the work.
objectives: Write a brief response that addresses a specific interaction and returns to the work.
Identify an intervention that publicly burdens the affected person.
Distinguish an immediate response from formal investigation or determination.
takeaways: A clear interruption can be brief.
Do not make the affected person perform an explanation.
Immediate action does not complete formal handling.
lessons.statement: A leader can set a clear work boundary without turning a colleague’s experience into a public lesson.

image.caption: A brief response can interrupt the interaction and preserve participation.

intro.heading: Address the action and the work expectation
intro.body:
Leaders sometimes remain silent because they do not know whether the interaction was intended to harm. Others respond with a long public speech that makes the affected person the center of attention. A proportionate immediate response can be brief and specific: identify the action that needs to stop or change, state the relevant work expectation and preserve a useful way to continue. Serious safety or policy matters require their responsible procedures; this practice is not a universal script for every incident.

Consider a name-related exchange. A leader might say, “Use the name our colleague has asked us to use. Let us return to the review question.” This addresses the behavior without inviting the room to vote on whether the colleague is entitled to concern. It does not make a legal finding or require a personal cultural explanation.

Avoid putting the burden on the person affected. Do not ask them to explain why everyone should care, demonstrate harm or accept an apology publicly to keep the meeting moving. They may choose to contribute, but the leader should not make that choice a condition of respectful participation. If the situation needs a pause, explain the practical next step without revealing unnecessary personal information.

An immediate response and formal handling are different. A short intervention may stop the interaction, while a concern still needs timely routing and the leader’s actual duties. Do not promise that the issue is resolved because the meeting resumed. Obtain current HR or responsible guidance for the specific facts, and preserve appropriate records.

Reflect on proportionality. A clear boundary should not become humiliation or a diagnosis of the speaker’s character. At the same time, avoiding humiliation does not mean avoiding accountability. State the behavior and expectation in plain terms, use suitable support and follow the process needed for the actual concern.

inThisLesson: Keep safety and formal routes clear.
Avoid declaring the issue resolved prematurely.
lessons.keyStatement: Interrupt the behavior, state the expectation and preserve the right next process.

items.title: A brief correction is possible
items.body: Address the specific action in understandable words and move back to the task when appropriate. The response should not depend on proving the speaker’s motive. Check afterward through the responsible process rather than assuming that a short correction completed every duty.

items.title: The room begins debating the person’s concern
items.body: Stop the debate that makes respectful participation conditional on public persuasion. Clarify the relevant work expectation and provide an appropriate next route. The affected person should not have to convince every colleague before the leader addresses the interaction.

items.title: The situation raises serious safety or policy questions
items.body: Use the actual responsible procedures and obtain appropriate help. Do not rely on a conversational script when formal action is needed. Explain the immediate practical step without making unsupported findings or disclosing private detail unnecessarily.

tabs.label: Action
tabs.body: Action names what needs to stop or change. A brief request to use the colleague’s stated name can address the exchange without making them explain their identity. Focus on the behavior rather than a cultural diagnosis. A proportionate intervention protects participation while retaining the need for appropriate follow-up and any applicable reporting.

tabs.label: Expectation
tabs.body: An expectation explains the relevant conduct or work boundary. The room should not vote on whether a colleague deserves respectful treatment. State the behavior required in understandable terms and avoid a public speech that makes the affected person a spectacle. Clear accountability does not require an improvised character judgment or a compulsory educational presentation.

tabs.label: Next step
tabs.body: The next step restores the task when appropriate or explains a practical pause and proper route. A resumed meeting does not prove the concern is resolved. Managers retain applicable reporting duties, including immediate reporting under Policy 1436 where a protected-class allegation or incident arises. Keep the intervention and formal handling distinct so neither is lost.

check.question: A leader wants the affected colleague to explain their experience to the whole meeting before intervening. What is the concern?
check.correct: The response places a public educational burden on the colleague rather than the leader addressing the interaction and responsible next step.
wrong: Every concern requires a public personal presentation before action.
The colleague must accept any explanation to keep the meeting moving.
The leader can avoid all responsibility until motive is fully established.
check.feedbackCorrect: The leader can address a clear work expectation without making the colleague perform a public defense.
check.feedbackIncorrect: A public personal presentation is not a prerequisite for a leader to address an observed interaction. Compelling acceptance pressures the colleague to supply closure. Waiting indefinitely for proven motive can leave a clear work boundary unenforced. Respond to the behavior proportionately and retain the formal route or reporting duty where needed.

items.text: Ask colleagues to use the requested name and return to the task.
Require the employee to explain their cultural identity to the room.
Seek the designated process for a serious reported concern.
Stop the repeated interruption and clarify the participation expectation.
Humiliate the speaker with an unsupported character diagnosis.
Follow actual safety procedures when the situation requires them.

lessons.next: Next, listen privately without promising secrecy or directing the person’s choice.

scenario.context: DSD practice case: In a meeting, Elise repeatedly interrupts colleague Mateo and makes a remark about who is “naturally” suited for analysis. Supervisor Farah asks Mateo to explain the harm to everyone before she will respond. The discussion is becoming a debate about Mateo.
scenario.prompt: Which immediate response is more useful?
options: Stop the public burden, address the interaction and participation expectation briefly, and follow the appropriate next process.
Require Mateo to persuade the room before allowing his contribution.
Announce a final legal conclusion during the meeting.
responses: This preserves participation and the leader’s responsibility without turning the meeting into an improvised adjudication.
The colleague should not have to perform a public defense to receive a proportionate response.
A meeting intervention does not establish every fact or the formal outcome.

lessons.transfer: Write a two-sentence response to an invented interaction: specific behavior, relevant expectation and practical next step. Identify any formal question the script cannot decide.

move.control: You can address the interaction and obtain appropriate help without making a public spectacle.
move.failure: The leader’s response either leaves the behavior untouched or creates another burden for the colleague.
move.next: Prepare one brief work-boundary phrase and know the responsible route for situations it cannot resolve.

lessons.title: Listen without making support conditional on disclosure
lessons.summary: Invite the person’s account and practical needs while explaining actual duties, privacy limits and routes.
lessons.objective: Write a neutral check-in that gives the person choice about what to share.
objectives: Write a neutral check-in that gives the person choice about what to share.
Distinguish practical support from directing a formal complaint outcome.
takeaways: Explain actual privacy and duty limits.
Do not require a personal story or preferred response.
lessons.statement: A helpful check-in gives someone a clear route without requiring them to make the leader comfortable.

image.caption: A private check-in can clarify needs without requiring unnecessary personal disclosure.

intro.heading: Ask what would support the person’s work
intro.body:
After an interaction, a leader may want immediate reassurance that everyone is fine. The affected person may feel pressure to accept that message, recount private experiences or decide what should happen to the speaker. A useful check-in focuses on the person’s account, participation and practical support, while explaining the leader’s actual responsibilities and the available formal routes.

Ask a neutral question such as, “I heard that exchange and addressed it. Is there anything about your work or participation that you want me to understand, and would an appropriate support route be useful?” The person may want to share, may prefer another contact or may not want a personal conversation. Do not make disclosure a condition of respectful treatment or expect the person to represent a community.

Explain privacy accurately. A leader may have duties to act or share information through an authorized process. Do not promise complete secrecy or invent an off-the-record option. Seek current guidance about actual records and communication. Course practice should use practice accounts rather than real personnel details or sensitive history.

Separate support from a desired outcome. The person need not forgive, accept an apology or choose an informal conversation to obtain help. Likewise, a general check-in should not become an improvised finding about another employee. Formal concerns and applicable rights follow their designated processes. Explain the route and follow duties that apply, without making the person responsible for designing the agency’s response.

Ask about practical work arrangements within your authority. Can the person contribute to the next meeting? Is a clear contact or suitable support useful? Avoid punitive or isolating changes made under the label of protection. A supportive conversation should preserve the person’s agency and fair access, while the leader carries out the responsibilities that remain theirs.

For covered managers and supervisors, MMB Policy 1436 requires immediate reporting of protected-class harassment or discrimination allegations or incidents to human resources or the agency Affirmative Action Officer, followed by current agency procedures. A learning exercise, check-in or optional repair conversation does not postpone that duty. Other matters follow their applicable policy and responsible route; do not conduct a course-based investigation.

lessons.keyStatement: Support is not a bargain for disclosure, forgiveness or silence.

items.title: The leader wants reassurance
items.body: Do not ask the person to say everything is fine so the leader can close the matter. Invite a relevant account and explain practical support. The person’s comfort with a conversation is not the only evidence, and declining to share does not remove the leader’s applicable responsibilities.

items.title: The leader promises secrecy
items.body: Check actual duties and record rules before making a statement about privacy. Explain the appropriate process in familiar terms and seek responsible guidance. A well-meant promise that cannot be kept can undermine trust more than a clear, honest limit.

items.title: Support changes the person’s opportunity
items.body: Removing the person from a useful meeting or project may isolate them rather than help. Ask about practical needs and use responsible guidance for actual changes. Support should not quietly reduce fair access or become a response to the person’s protected concern.

tabs.label: Account
tabs.body: An account invites the information the person chooses to share about the interaction and work effect. It is not a demand for personal history or an explanation of a whole community. A neutral check-in can reveal a participation issue while respecting preference for another contact. Support should not depend on an elaborate public defense.

tabs.label: Process
tabs.body: The process explains appropriate routes and information limits accurately. Do not promise absolute confidentiality or ask the employee to decide whether you fulfill your own duties. Covered managers must immediately report protected-class harassment or discrimination allegations or incidents under Policy 1436. A private check-in can support the person, but cannot substitute for required handling.

tabs.label: Support
tabs.body: Support concerns a practical arrangement within authority, such as maintaining a useful role in the review. Removing an opportunity to quiet a concern may compound the problem. Discuss a suitable response without requiring silence, forgiveness or a private narrative. Preserve the employee’s agency while keeping legitimate work requirements and formal decisions in their responsible processes.

check.question: A supervisor says they will help only if the employee agrees not to report the concern. What should change?
check.correct: Offer appropriate support and follow responsible processes without making silence a condition.
wrong: Keep the bargain because it may reduce conflict.
Require a public apology acceptance before providing help.
Remove the employee from development opportunities for raising the issue.
check.feedbackCorrect: Support and formal process should not become conditional on silence, forgiveness or a hidden penalty.
check.feedbackIncorrect: A bargain for silence can suppress the responsible route. Compulsory apology acceptance does not establish support or repair. Removing development access because an employee raised a concern can compound it and requires responsible scrutiny. Offer appropriate support without these conditions and fulfill actual reporting and process duties.

items.text: Offer a useful contact and ask what would support participation.
Promise that no information will ever be shared regardless of duties.
Require silence before offering support.
Explain the actual route and invite only what the person chooses to share.
Guarantee a formal outcome before the concern is examined.
Make forgiveness the price of continued project access.

lessons.next: Next, address expectations with the person whose conduct needs attention.

scenario.context: DSD practice case: Supervisor Jo checks in with Nadia after an exclusionary remark. Jo offers to remove Nadia from a visible project so she will not have to attend the meetings, and asks her to keep the concern private. Nadia wants continued access and a clear support route.
options: Insist that removal is protection and requires no discussion.
Discuss appropriate support and participation, explain the responsible route and avoid conditioning help on silence or reducing access improperly.
Ask Nadia to decide the disciplinary result during the check-in.
responses: A protective intention does not make an isolating change appropriate.
This preserves agency, practical support and responsible formal handling.
The employee’s account matters, but the formal decision follows its responsible process.

lessons.transfer: Draft a practice check-in with a neutral invitation, accurate privacy limit, formal route and practical participation question. Remove any condition of silence or forgiveness.

move.control: You can offer support and explain routes without demanding disclosure or directing the person’s emotional response.
move.failure: The check-in asks the employee to protect the leader’s comfort or give up an opportunity.
move.next: Use an accurate, choice-preserving support statement after the next relevant interaction.

lessons.title: Clarify conduct expectations without diagnosing character
lessons.summary: Address a specific action and its work effect through the appropriate supervisory process.
lessons.objective: Write feedback that connects an observed interaction to a relevant expectation.
objectives: Write feedback that connects an observed interaction to a relevant expectation.
Identify when a conduct discussion requires responsible HR guidance.
Distinguish accountability from humiliation or an individual cultural label.
takeaways: Accountability does not require a character diagnosis.
lessons.statement: A clear conversation explains what must change and why, without deciding who the person is.

image.caption: Specific conduct feedback is more useful than a broad personal label.

intro.heading: Make the expectation and next action clear
intro.body:
A leader may avoid a conduct conversation because they fear accusing someone of bad intent. Another may confront the person with a broad label that leaves no clear path to change. A responsible discussion focuses on the observed interaction, relevant expectation, work effect and practical next step. Actual concerns may require HR or another designated process; a learning script does not replace those duties.

Prepare the account accurately. What did you hear or receive, what remains uncertain and which expectation is relevant? Do not rely on gossip or assume every reported detail is established. Follow responsible procedures for obtaining and handling information. Use the example to examine the wording without creating a real personnel record.

Explain the behavior and work connection. For example, repeated interruption can prevent another person’s contribution from being considered. A name-related comment can need a clear correction and appropriate follow-through. Do not claim that a single conversation proves the speaker’s entire character, culture or developmental orientation. The person can be accountable for behavior without such a diagnosis.

Listen to a relevant response while retaining the standard. A person may supply context or identify a misunderstanding that needs examination. “I meant well” is information about stated intent, not automatic proof that the effect or expectation disappears. A fair response can acknowledge intent and still require an appropriate change.

Agree on a specific action and follow the actual supervisory process. If formal investigation, documentation or employment action is needed, use its responsible authority. Do not improvise discipline, require a coerced apology or make optional learning an unapproved employment condition. Useful learning support can be offered while formal responsibilities remain clear and the leader checks whether the behavior changes.

lessons.keyStatement: The conversation connects behavior, effect and required work practice rather than a diagnosis of identity or character.

items.title: “That was not my intention”
items.body: Acknowledge the stated intent without using it to erase the interaction or effect. Clarify the expectation and appropriate next action. If context changes the facts, examine it through the responsible process. Do not force an admission of motive as the only route to a practical correction.

items.title: The leader wants a public confession
items.body: Humiliation is not a useful substitute for accountability. Follow actual supervisory and formal procedures, explain the conduct expectation and preserve appropriate privacy. A course exercise does not authorize a public disciplinary performance or guarantee that an apology resolves the concern.

items.title: A formal question appears
items.body: Seek current HR or designated guidance rather than treating the conversation as an investigation. Keep records and evidence in approved channels. The leader should understand the route and applicable responsibilities without inventing thresholds, sanctions or a separate informal complaint system.

tabs.label: Account
tabs.body: An account separates observed detail, reported experience and unresolved information. That distinction allows the leader to take a concern seriously without announcing every fact as settled. Actual records belong in approved channels. A course exercise uses practice information and cannot determine the speaker’s motives, legal responsibility or assessed intercultural-development orientation.

tabs.label: Expectation
tabs.body: An expectation connects a specific action to a relevant work or conduct requirement. Explain the behavior that must change instead of calling someone culturally deficient. Accountability can be firm without staging a confession or requiring the affected employee to administer it. If the facts raise a formal concern, preserve the responsible route alongside the immediate boundary.

tabs.label: Next step
tabs.body: A next step identifies an action within authority and the formal matters another role handles. A clear conversation may explain what is expected without resolving the allegation or determining discipline. State the real review point and keep personal information appropriately limited. Do not use a public promise or inferred developmental score as the measure of compliance.

check.question: A leader says a colleague’s remark proves their IDI orientation and asks for a public confession. What is the better approach?
check.correct: Address the specific behavior and relevant expectation through responsible procedures without diagnosing an orientation or staging humiliation.
wrong: Use the inferred orientation as a personnel score.
Require the affected employee to administer the conduct response.
Ignore the behavior because motive is not fully known.
check.feedbackCorrect: Accountability can be clear and specific without a cultural diagnosis or inappropriate public performance.
check.feedbackIncorrect: An inferred IDI orientation cannot become a personnel score. Asking the affected employee to administer the response transfers the leader’s responsibility. Ignoring an observed behavior merely because motive remains uncertain also leaves the work issue unattended. State the relevant conduct expectation and use appropriate procedures without diagnosis or humiliation.

items.text: Explain that the repeated interruption prevented contribution and state the participation expectation.
Assign a permanent cultural label from one exchange.
Seek designated HR guidance for an actual formal concern.
Identify the required change in name use and appropriate follow-up.
Require a public confession to prove the leader acted.
Keep actual conduct records in approved channels.

lessons.next: Next, examine repair without coercion or process substitution.

scenario.context: DSD practice case: Supervisor Alex speaks with Celeste about a repeated dismissive comment. Celeste says she intended efficiency. Alex is tempted to label her cultural orientation and require a public apology immediately. The actual concern needs current supervisory guidance.
options: Treat stated intent as proof there is nothing to address.
Have the affected colleague determine every sanction.
Explain the observed behavior and expectation, examine relevant context and follow responsible guidance without diagnosis or public coercion.
responses: Intent does not automatically remove a work effect or conduct expectation.
The affected person should not carry the agency’s supervisory or formal decision responsibility.
This preserves accountability, evidence and appropriate process without an unsupported personal label.

lessons.transfer: Write practice conduct feedback with account, uncertainty, expectation, work effect and next action. Identify the formal questions you must route rather than decide.

move.control: You can clarify a relevant expectation and follow responsible procedures without inferring identity or motive.
move.failure: The discussion either dismisses the effect or turns accountability into humiliation and cultural labeling.
move.next: Before the next conduct discussion, check its evidence, expectation and responsible process route.

lessons.title: Support repair without requiring forgiveness
lessons.summary: Distinguish useful corrective action from a forced interpersonal settlement or substitute for formal handling.
lessons.objective: Identify a repair action connected to the actual work effect.
objectives: Identify a repair action connected to the actual work effect.
Explain why apology or forgiveness cannot be treated as the sole evidence of resolution.
Distinguish an optional appropriate conversation from a mandatory informal barrier to formal routes.
takeaways: Repair addresses the effect and future practice.
Forgiveness is not a work requirement created here.
lessons.statement: A useful correction changes what happens next; it does not require the affected person to declare everything resolved.

image.caption: Practical repair focuses on the work effect and future behavior.

intro.heading: Choose an action that matches the effect
intro.body:
After an interaction, people may want a quick apology so the team can move on. An apology can matter, but it is not the same as repairing a work effect or completing the responsible process. A colleague whose contribution was ignored may need the analysis reconsidered. A person repeatedly interrupted may need a clearer participation practice. A forced statement of forgiveness does not establish that either change occurred.

Begin with the actual effect and appropriate authority. What work was interrupted, information dismissed or opportunity reduced? Identify a corrective action within the leader’s role and follow the designated process for formal concerns. Do not use a learning conversation to settle matters that require investigation or a specialized decision.

An interpersonal conversation may be useful when appropriate, safe and consistent with current procedures. It should not be imposed as a universal requirement before someone can use a formal route. Power differences and the person’s preferences matter. Seek responsible guidance rather than treating mediation or a group discussion as the automatic response to every concern.

Keep responsibility with the person and role that own the action. The speaker may need to change a behavior; the leader may need to improve a meeting arrangement; a process owner may need to revisit a decision. Do not ask the affected employee to design all repair, teach the team or accept a prescribed emotional response. Their account can inform the action without transferring the agency’s responsibility.

Check the result through appropriate evidence. Did the dismissed contribution receive consideration? Did the interruption stop? Is participation usable without new isolation or pressure? A positive conversation is relevant but should not conceal remaining concerns. Formal records and actual employment actions remain in approved channels; these course activities use practice cases and do not certify resolution.

lessons.keyStatement: Repair is demonstrated through appropriate action and follow-through, not a compelled declaration that the issue is over.

items.title: A scripted apology is the whole plan
items.body: An apology may be one part of a response, but ask what will change in the work. A useful action addresses the effect, such as reconsidering a contribution or clarifying a participation practice. Do not make an apology a certificate that every formal issue has been resolved.

items.title: A conversation is required before reporting
items.body: This course does not create such a barrier. Current policy and responsible procedures determine available routes and duties. Explain the actual options and seek guidance rather than imposing mediation or direct confrontation universally. Optional dialogue should not be a price for formal support.

items.title: The affected person must teach the team
items.body: That requirement can add another burden. Use established resources and appropriate expertise for learning. Invite any contribution genuinely and keep the person’s choice meaningful. The leader and responsible roles still own corrective action and appropriate process.

tabs.label: Work
tabs.body: Work identifies the contribution or opportunity affected. If a colleague’s evidence was dismissed, consider its proper review; a ceremonial apology cannot substitute for that decision. Keep the correction tied to the effect. This makes repair practical without promising adoption of the person’s proposal or requiring them to pronounce the whole situation resolved.

tabs.label: Responsibility
tabs.body: Responsibility names the behavior or arrangement to change and the role that can do it. The affected employee should not become responsible for every future training session or for monitoring all conduct. Preserve actual formal handling and decision authority. The leader owns an appropriate response even when the person does not choose to forgive or participate in an informal conversation.

tabs.label: Follow-through
tabs.body: Follow-through checks whether the action was delivered and whether participation improved. Silence may mean several things and cannot certify success. Offer a suitable feedback route without compelling another personal account. If the barrier remains, revisit the arrangement or use responsible guidance; do not require emotional closure to make the report look complete.

check.question: A leader requires the affected employee to accept a public apology before returning to a project. What should change?
check.correct: Remove the coerced condition, preserve appropriate project access and use responsible guidance for corrective action and formal handling.
wrong: Keep the condition because it creates visible closure.
Treat apology acceptance as the only possible evidence of repair.
Make the employee responsible for all future training about the incident.
check.feedbackCorrect: Participation and support should not depend on a prescribed emotional response or compulsory educational role.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Visible closure does not justify coercing apology acceptance. An emotional statement is not the only possible evidence of a work correction. Making the employee responsible for all training transfers another burden. Remove the condition, preserve appropriate participation and seek responsible guidance for correction and formal handling.

items.text: Reconsider a dismissed contribution through the appropriate review.
Require forgiveness before continued project access.
Confirm whether an actual concern needs designated formal handling.
Clarify turn-taking and check whether contribution becomes usable.
Declare the issue over because a public apology was performed.
Do not impose informal mediation as a new universal reporting prerequisite.

lessons.next: Next, examine patterns and improve leadership follow-through.

scenario.context: DSD practice case: At a review, Sonia’s evidence was dismissed through an exclusionary remark. Leader Devon arranges an apology but does not return the evidence to the decision process. He asks Sonia to say the matter is resolved before she rejoins the project.
options: Preserve appropriate participation, revisit the evidence through its responsible review and follow the formal route without requiring a resolution statement.
Keep the apology as the complete proof of repair.
Ask Sonia to teach the team before her evidence can be considered.
responses: This addresses the work effect and preserves agency and responsible handling.
An apology does not by itself establish that the evidence or participation issue was corrected.
The employee’s contribution should not depend on compulsory cultural education.

lessons.transfer: Build a practice repair plan with effect, corrective action, responsible owner, formal boundary and check. Remove any requirement for forgiveness or public personal disclosure.

move.control: You can address work effects and arrange responsible follow-through without prescribing a person’s emotional response.
move.failure: A visible apology becomes a substitute for changed behavior, fair access and proper process.
move.next: For the next appropriate correction, identify the work effect and how its repair will actually be checked.

lessons.title: Review patterns without profiling people
lessons.summary: Learn from appropriate evidence while avoiding retaliation, identity assumptions and unsupported success claims.
lessons.objective: Identify process evidence that can inform a leadership improvement.
objectives: Identify process evidence that can inform a leadership improvement.
Explain why silence or few reports does not prove absence of concerns.
Choose a practical improvement with an owner and an appropriate result check.
takeaways: Missing reports do not establish a healthy climate.
Do not create personal cultural scores.
lessons.statement: The aim is a more dependable workplace response, not a dashboard that classifies colleagues.

image.caption: A careful review connects evidence, limits and an accountable next action.

intro.heading: Improve the response system through practical evidence
intro.body:
A leader may want to prove that a team has no microaggressions by counting reports. A low count can reflect fewer problems, but it can also reflect uncertainty about routes, fear of consequences or a preference not to disclose. The figure alone does not establish a healthy climate. Review the arrangements that enable respectful participation and responsible handling, with appropriate privacy and evidence limits.

Choose a process question within authority. Do employees know the current concern route? Are leaders clear about immediate response and formal responsibilities? Are meeting contributions considered without representative burdens? Do corrective actions have owners and appropriate checks? These questions can support practical improvement without collecting every personal account or creating a new informal personnel database.

Use current responsible guidance for actual records and any pattern analysis. Small or distinctive situations may identify employees even without names. Do not invent a reporting threshold or record retention rule in this course. Formal complaint and employment data stay in approved channels; optional learning responses should not become a source of individual cultural or IDI labels.

Avoid adverse treatment in response to concerns or protected activity. EEOC guidance explains that applicable employment laws prohibit retaliation for protected activity; actual facts and policy questions need responsible advice. Do not interpret speaking up as low commitment, remove opportunities to make the problem disappear or increase scrutiny because someone raised a concern. Legitimate work responsibilities still follow their appropriate standards and procedures.

State what the evidence supports and what remains uncertain. An improved meeting arrangement can be a useful result without proving every concern has vanished. Choose a specific next action, responsible owner and result check. The Equity and Inclusion Operations Consultant can provide guidance and feedback while leaders and staff carry out their own responsibilities. Over time, credible follow-through is more useful than a confident statement that the team has eliminated every problem.

lessons.keyStatement: Examine the workplace response without turning concerns or learning participation into personal labels.

items.title: Few concerns are reported
items.body: The count needs context and cannot establish absence of harm by itself. Check whether routes are understandable and leaders respond credibly. Do not demand more personal disclosure merely to populate a chart. A process improvement can be useful while the broader prevalence remains unknown.

items.title: A person speaks up repeatedly
items.body: Examine each concern through its responsible route rather than labeling the person difficult or disloyal. Do not use reporting as a reason to remove fair opportunities. Legitimate performance matters remain separate and require relevant evidence and the appropriate procedure. Seek responsible guidance about actual retaliation questions.

items.title: A learning score appears on a personnel chart
items.body: Course activity does not establish cultural orientation or commitment. Remove unsupported personal inference from the learning purpose and follow actual data requirements. The program should build capacity and appropriate practice, not create hidden labels or gates from optional participation.

tabs.label: Finding
tabs.body: A finding states what the process evidence establishes. Fewer reports are a reporting pattern, not proof that every concern ended. A changed meeting arrangement may show a delivered step, while a suitable check can examine its effect. Keep those distinctions visible so the next decision responds to evidence rather than reassurance.

tabs.label: Limit
tabs.body: A limit explains missing information and privacy constraints. The leader cannot infer motive, commitment or an IDI orientation from who spoke in meetings. Unknown information is not a favorable result. Obtain appropriate data and process guidance and ask what can be examined safely, without turning a learning review into informal employee profiling.

tabs.label: Action
tabs.body: An action addresses a supported process gap with an owner and result check. A confusing concern route may need clearer instructions, while an actual allegation still needs its responsible handling. Staff do their work with consultant guidance rather than transfer every review to the consultant. A practical improvement is useful even when it cannot prove a universal workplace outcome.

check.question: A team has no recent reports, and the leader wants to declare all concerns eliminated. What is the responsible response?
check.correct: Describe the limited reporting evidence, examine whether routes and follow-through are usable, and avoid claiming absence of concerns from silence alone.
wrong: Assign low commitment to anyone who later raises a concern.
Fill the dashboard with reassuring symbols for unknown information.
Infer individual IDI orientations from who spoke during meetings.
check.feedbackCorrect: This retains the observation while acknowledging its limits and directing attention to a practical process inquiry.
check.feedbackIncorrect: A later concern cannot justify an unsupported low-commitment label. Reassuring dashboard symbols cannot fill unknown information. Speaking patterns cannot reveal assessed individual IDI orientations. State the reporting evidence and its limits, examine usable routes and follow-through, and choose an appropriate process improvement without profiling people.

items.text: Check whether employees can identify the current responsible concern route.
No recent reports proves every interaction was harmless.
Clarify a participation expectation and review its use at the next meeting.
Examine whether corrective actions have appropriate follow-through owners.
Reporting a concern proves low loyalty.
Provide leaders a clear distinction between immediate response and formal handling.

lessons.next: Use the job aid to notice, respond and follow through responsibly.

scenario.context: DSD practice case: Director Amira sees no recent reports and proposes a public success claim. Staff still do not know the current concern route, and one leader suggests removing a frequent reporter from visible work to improve the atmosphere.
options: Publish the claim and make the opportunity removal.
Clarify the route, examine response follow-through and seek responsible guidance on the proposed adverse treatment, while reporting evidence limits honestly.
Create cultural scores from optional course participation.
responses: Silence does not prove success, and the proposed adverse treatment needs responsible attention.
This addresses the practical gap and the actual formal concern without overclaiming or profiling.
Course activity does not diagnose culture or justify a personnel score.

lessons.transfer: Create a practice leadership-response improvement plan with process question, appropriate evidence, privacy limit, non-retaliatory check, owner and next action.

move.control: You can improve clarity and follow-through while keeping formal matters and employee information in responsible channels.
move.failure: A low report count becomes reassurance while people lose access or acquire hidden labels for speaking up.
move.next: Review one concern-route or participation arrangement and make an evidence-linked improvement with the responsible roles.

jobAid.subtitle: Notice the interaction, respond clearly and follow through through the right process.
remember: Separate observed behavior, reported effect and inferred motive.
Do not make the affected person perform public education or forgiveness.
Immediate response and formal handling are distinct responsibilities.

sections.heading: Notice and intervene
items: Describe the words or action accurately.
Use a brief, specific work-boundary response where appropriate.
Preserve safety, participation and current formal routes.

sections.heading: Listen and address
items: Offer a neutral check-in with accurate privacy limits.
Provide support without conditions of silence or disclosure.
Clarify conduct expectations through responsible supervisory procedures.
Avoid individual cultural or IDI labels and public humiliation.

sections.heading: Repair and review
items: Address the actual work effect, not just visible apology.
Do not impose an informal barrier to formal concerns.
Assign corrective action and appropriate result checks.
Keep real records in approved channels and protect recognizable situations.
Treat missing reports as limited evidence, and seek responsible guidance on retaliation or adverse treatment.
